intent: Declare that two bounded contexts do not integrate at all, and let each solve its own problem locally — paying duplication deliberately instead of paying coupling.
problem: An integration between two contexts looks valuable and costs far more than it returns: a shared abstraction, a translation layer, a coordinated roadmap and a release dependency, all for a capability neither side genuinely needs from the other.
context: Separate ways is the most under-used relationship on the context map, and the most often the correct one. It is the deliberate decision to duplicate functionality rather than integrate, justified by an explicit cost/benefit judgement: the cost of integration exceeds the benefit. Its sibling in the taxonomy is duplicate functionality, which it deliberately permits. Evans' three options when coordination with an upstream fails are: abandon the supplier (separate ways), take responsibility for translation (an ACL), or adopt the foreign model (conformist) — separate ways is the only one that removes the dependency.
benefits: The coupling is gone: neither team blocks the other, and both release independently.
Each context is free to model the problem in the way that suits it, in its own ubiquitous language.
No translation layer, no shared contract, no negotiated deprecation schedule.
The context map becomes smaller and more honest.
Duplicate code is a far cheaper failure mode than a distributed dependency.
tradeoffs: Functionality is duplicated, so both copies need fixing when the shared requirement changes.
The two models may drift, producing inconsistent answers to the same business question.
Deciding not to integrate is a positive claim that needs evidence; it is easy to use as an excuse.
Cross-context queries or reports must be assembled by hand or in a reporting context.
If the relationship is later needed, the duplication has to be undone before integration.
quality_attributes_note: scalability 9 and simplicity 9 — the two contexts are free. maintainability 6 because duplicate functionality has to be maintained twice; testability 9 because there is no seam to mock.

participants.responsibility: Solves its own version of the problem in its own language.
Solves the same problem differently, also independently.
participants.notes: The duplication is the accepted price.

participants.responsibility: The recorded judgement that integration cost exceeds benefit.
participants.notes: Without this record the choice looks like an omission.

use_cases: Two contexts needing a customer list but neither needing the other's internal representation.
A supplier whose model cannot be adapted and whose capabilities are not worth an anti-corruption layer.
Two teams with no release overlap and no realistic plan to coordinate.
An integration kept alive only by one rarely-used feature, whose coordination cost exceeds the feature's value.
avoid_when: The two contexts must agree on an answer for the business to be correct.
A change to the shared requirement must reach both copies at once.
The contexts are in the same codebase and release, where integration is nearly free.
The duplicated concept is a regulatory or accounting rule, which must have exactly one interpretation.
pitfalls: Choosing it as a default to avoid the hard conversation about boundaries.
Duplicating without recording the decision, so someone later "fixes" it with an unwanted integration.
Duplicating a rule that must be consistent, rather than a presentation that may differ.
Allowing the two copies to converge into a shared library by accident, quietly becoming a shared kernel.
Ignoring the cross-context report that the duplication made impossible to build.

related_patterns_notes.conformist: Conformist keeps the dependency and removes the model; separate ways removes both.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: The ACL is the option taken when the supplier cannot be abandoned but the model is unacceptable.
related_patterns_notes.shared-kernel: The opposite bet: that coordination is cheaper than duplication.

anti_patterns: Separate ways declared for two contexts that must produce consistent answers.
Duplicated business rules that change together and must change in step.
A separate-ways decision never recorded, so it is undone by the next well-meaning engineer.
Two copies that converge on a shared implementation and become a shared kernel without anyone deciding that.
design_principles: Separate Ways: a bounded context with no connection to the others at all, allowing developers to find simple, specialized solutions within this small scope (Evans, via Wikipedia).
Only integrate if we really need to; otherwise keep them completely isolated (Graca).
When coordination with a supplier is impossible, the three options are abandon the supplier, take responsibility for translation, or adopt the foreign model.
A context map should show relationships deliberately chosen, including deliberate non-integration.
best_practices: Record the decision and its reasoning on the context map, so it is visible as a choice.
Name the trigger that would reopen the question (a new requirement, a reorganisation, a contract change).
When duplication is chosen, duplicate the presentation, not a rule that must have one interpretation.
Build the cross-context report in a reporting context rather than re-coupling the two.
Revisit the decision whenever either context's model changes significantly.
